title: Boss: the double-reminder incident
summary: Customers got two overdue reminders. Pin the reminder job with fakes, fake time and a mock; replace an over-mocked test that broke on a harmless refactor; and test random coupon codes by their properties.

steps.title: Incident INC-2291: two reminders per invoice
body: Support forwards complaints: customers received the same "invoice overdue" e-mail twice, an hour apart. The job runs hourly. Its log:

The second run sent the same 41 reminders again, then a hotfix went out. The post-incident review asks for tests that would have caught it, and for the other ways this job can annoy customers: reminding too early, reminding paid invoices.

Plan the doubles before writing anything: the invoice store is **read and written** by the job (a fake keeps it honest), the mailer is an **outgoing side effect** (a mock or a spy), and "overdue" depends on **today** (a fake clock).

steps.title: Pin the reminder job
prompt: The job, compiled beside your tests:
public record Invoice(int Id, string Email, DateOnly Due, bool Paid);
public interface IInvoices { IReadOnlyList<Invoice> Open(); bool WasReminded(int id); void MarkReminded(int id); }
public interface IMailer { void Send(string to, string subject); }
public class ReminderJob(IInvoices invoices, IMailer mailer, TimeProvider clock)
// An invoice gets one reminder, once it is 3 days past its due date and still unpaid.
- `public sealed class FakeInvoices : IInvoices` (an in-memory list of invoices and a set of reminded ids);
- `public class ReminderJobTests` with at least **five** tests using your fake, `Substitute.For<IMailer>()` and a `FakeTimeProvider`. One test must reproduce the incident: two runs, one e-mail.
Six planted bugs, including the one from the incident.
starter: public IReadOnlyList<Invoice> Open() => throw new NotImplementedException();
public bool WasReminded(int id) => throw new NotImplementedException();
public void MarkReminded(int id) => throw new NotImplementedException();
solution: readonly FakeTimeProvider clock = new(new DateTimeOffset(2026, 11, 24, 9, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero));

target: public record Invoice(int Id, string Email, DateOnly Due, bool Paid);
public interface IInvoices { IReadOnlyList<Invoice> Open(); bool WasReminded(int id); void MarkReminded(int id); }
public interface IMailer { void Send(string to, string subject); }
public class ReminderJob(IInvoices invoices, IMailer mailer, TimeProvider clock)

mutants.name: the incident: reminded invoices are reminded again
mutants.hint: Run the job twice on the same store and expect one e-mail.

mutants.name: reminders go out a day early
mutants.hint: An invoice 2 days overdue must not get a reminder yet.

mutants.name: reminders wait a day too long
mutants.hint: An invoice exactly 3 days overdue gets one.

require.message: Uses a FakeTimeProvider with an explicit start

hints: The fake is three one-liners: `Open() => Invoices`, `WasReminded(id) => Reminded.Contains(id)`, `MarkReminded(id) => Reminded.Add(id)`.
Fix today with `new FakeTimeProvider(new DateTimeOffset(2026, 11, 24, 9, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero))` and build due dates from it: exactly 3 days overdue gets a reminder, 2 days does not.
The incident test: add one overdue invoice, call `Run()` twice on the same fake (advance the clock an hour between), then `mailer.Received(1).Send(Arg.Any<string>(), Arg.Any<string>())`.
steps.explain: The fake store remembers across runs exactly like the database does, which is what makes the incident reproducible in a unit test. The mailer is the one true side effect, so it is the one thing verified with `Received`.

steps.title: Review: the test that broke on a harmless refactor
prompt: PR #318 made quotes faster: one batched `FindMany` instead of one `Find` per product. Prices did not change, but this old test went red, and the author wants to delete it. You suggest rewriting it instead.
The new code, compiled beside your tests:
public record Product(string Sku, decimal Price);
public static decimal Total(IProducts products, IReadOnlyDictionary<string, int> basket)
if (!found.TryGetValue(sku, out var p)) throw new KeyNotFoundException($"Unknown product {sku}.");
if (qty <= 0) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(basket), $"Quantity of {sku} must be positive.");

Replace the over-mocked test with a hand-written `public sealed class FakeProducts : IProducts` (built from a list of products, both methods working) and at least **four** state-based tests in `QuoteTests`: totals, an unknown product, a zero quantity. No `Received` checks: how the quote looks prices up is its own business. Four planted bugs.
starter: var total = Quote.Total(products, new Dictionary<string, int> { ["mug"] = 2, ["tea"] = 1 });
solution: public sealed class FakeProducts(params Product[] products) : IProducts
public Product? Find(string sku) => products.FirstOrDefault(p => p.Sku == sku);
public IReadOnlyList<Product> FindMany(IReadOnlyCollection<string> skus) => products.Where(p => skus.Contains(p.Sku)).ToList();
readonly FakeProducts products = new(new Product("mug", 8m), new Product("tea", 4.5m), new Product("pot", 24m));
var total = Quote.Total(products, new Dictionary<string, int> { ["mug"] = 2, ["tea"] = 1 });
var ex = Assert.Throws<KeyNotFoundException>(() => Quote.Total(products, new Dictionary<string, int> { ["mug"] = 1, ["cup"] = 1 }));

target: public record Product(string Sku, decimal Price);
public static decimal Total(IProducts products, IReadOnlyDictionary<string, int> basket)
if (!found.TryGetValue(sku, out var p)) throw new KeyNotFoundException($"Unknown product {sku}.");
if (qty <= 0) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(basket), $"Quantity of {sku} must be positive.");

forbid.message: No interaction checks on lookups (they are queries)

hints: Run checks on the starter first: it fails on the *correct* code. Read why: the substitute's `FindMany` returns an empty list.
A fake built from a list answers both methods truthfully: `FindMany(skus) => products.Where(p => skus.Contains(p.Sku)).ToList()`.
Assert on the total (two different items, one with quantity 2), and on the two exceptions.
steps.explain: The old test failed for a change that broke nothing, which teaches a team to ignore red tests. The fake answers both lookups truthfully, so the new tests survive any lookup strategy and still catch every pricing bug.

steps.title: Random coupon codes, tested by their properties
prompt: Marketing prints coupon codes on flyers, so they must be easy to type. The generator, compiled beside your tests:
public static IReadOnlyList<string> Generate(Random rng, int count)
for (int i = 0; i < chars.Length; i++) chars[i] = Alphabet[rng.Next(Alphabet.Length)];

Write `public class CouponCodeTests` with at least **four** tests. Do not assert exact codes (they depend on the algorithm). Assert **properties** of a large seeded batch instead (`new Random(2026)`, 1,000 codes): how many, how long, which characters (write the forbidden ones yourself, do not reuse `CouponCodes.Alphabet`), all different; plus that the same seed gives the same codes and that `count` must be positive. Five planted bugs.
solution: static readonly IReadOnlyList<string> Batch = CouponCodes.Generate(new Random(2026), 1000);

target: public static IReadOnlyList<string> Generate(Random rng, int count)
for (int i = 0; i < chars.Length; i++) chars[i] = Alphabet[rng.Next(Alphabet.Length)];

mutants.name: look-alike characters are back
mutants.hint: Check the characters against a pattern you wrote, such as ^[A-HJ-NP-Z2-9]+$, not against CouponCodes.Alphabet.

mutants.name: the last character is never filled in
the injected Random is ignored
mutants.hint: The same seed must give the same codes: that is the point of injecting the Random.

mutants.name: a count of zero is accepted

forbid.message: Expected characters come from the specification, not from CouponCodes.Alphabet

hints: Generate one seeded batch of 1,000 in a static field and assert on all of it with `Assert.All(batch, code => ...)`.
The allowed characters as a pattern: `^[A-HJ-NP-Z2-9]+$` (A to H, J to N, P to Z, 2 to 9).
`Assert.Equal(CouponCodes.Generate(new Random(7), 20), CouponCodes.Generate(new Random(7), 20));` proves the injected Random is used.
steps.explain: Property tests on a big seeded batch catch real bugs without freezing the algorithm: switch to another random source or a smarter loop and they still pass. The seed makes a failure reproducible; module 8 takes this idea further with Hypothesis.
